utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are continuing with Case No. IT-95-12-1. Is the Prosecutor ready to continue from yesterday evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. We have just one more witness to introduce in this 61 hearing, Lieutenant Colonel Koet of the Dutch Army, and Mr. Cayley will examine him. LIEUTENANT COLONEL JAN KOET, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have an oath? Would you please stand and give the oath?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. (The witness was sworn)

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Can I proceed, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by MR. CAYLEY

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed for coming this afternoon, Colonel. If I can just confirm a few preliminary matters with you? Your name is Jan Koet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you are a Lieutenant Colonel in the Dutch Army; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think in 1971 you attended the Royal Dutch Military Academy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1976 to 1978 you were a cavalry platoon commander in Germany; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1978 to 1980 I think you were the second-in-command of a cavalry squadron in Germany; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1980 to 1982 you commanded a squadron of tanks in Holland; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From 1982 to 1984 you were a staff officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in 1984 you attended the Dutch Army Staff College; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then in 1986 I understand you were allowed by the Dutch Army to study law full-time at Leiden University; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe in 1990 you were assigned as legal adviser to the commander of the 41st Dutch Army Brigade stationed in Germany; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it is correct that in 1993 you were assigned as the legal adviser to the commander of the UN Protection Force of Bosnia-Herzegovina headquartered in Kiseljak who was at the time Lieutenant General Briquemont; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it was a fairly large headquarters; how many people did it consist of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had about 600 people in that hotel from, I think, 10 nationalities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you said in your statement that within two months of arriving in the town of Kiseljak you noticed a change, and I wondered if you could explain to the court what you noticed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were allowed in the beginning to leave the compound, not to go shopping, but, well, if we had to do something we were allowed to go out. We were, for instance, allowed to do jogging around the hotel. But so now and then there was some shooting and that those incidents increased, and I think after two months we were not allowed to leave the compound at all except for on duty, and always all the time the two of us, at least.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Around 23rd or 24th October 1993, I think, you attended an important meeting at the headquarters in Kiseljak. I think Colonel Alstrom, who was the Assistant Chief of Staff in G3 Operations was there. I think, were you given a briefing by a UN military observer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court what that briefing was about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had to meet with several people and the legal adviser, Colonel Alstrom, as you mentioned. I think the G2 was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you explain to the court what the "G2" is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He is responsible for intelligence information gathering and, of course, the UNMO, Patrick Martin -- Lieutenant Colonel, I think was his rank -- and he said: "There is something very badly happened in a small village called Stupni Do. I was there today and I am very much afraid that people will become aware of that. At the moment we have still 10 to 12 UNMOs over there, and I am afraid that if the Bosnian Croats are becoming aware of the fact that they are still out there, they might be endangered". So he said: "I do not want you to talk about these things", and then he explained how he went to Stupni Do in the end with the commander mentioned, Ivica Rajic, and he explained how he did that. Do you want me to .....

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, if you could explain that to the court, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He knew that something terrible had happened in that village, and he also knew that Ivica Rajic was the responsible commander. He knew him before, so he went to the place where he was and he asked him permission to go in Stupni Do, the village. Well, at first, Ivica Rajic said: "Well, it is not possible". It was a very tense situation, and he looked very nervous -- I remember he said it to me -- and then he asked if it was possible to enter that village, to go into that village, with one of his officers. Ivica Rajic said: "No, well, it is not possible but, no, we cannot do that". Then interpreter suddenly said: "Well, why do you not go yourself?" And, to their surprise, he said: "OK, I will go with you". So they went, I do not know whether it was in one car or more car, they went to the village and when Patrick Martin came there he saw that everything was burning, still burning and then smelling and there was smoke. He asked permission to enter a house. At first Ivica Rajic did not want him to do that, but in the end he said: "OK, you can go into one house". So Patrick Martin went into one house and he did not see anything. Yes, he said he saw that things were burned and demolished, etc. Then he asked for permission to go into a second house and there he discovered a dead man, I think, behind a door, a wooden staircase -- I cannot remember precisely. So he was very much afraid when he saw that and went back to Ivica Rajic and he, Ivica Rajic, asked: "Well, what did you see?" He said: "Well, I did not see anything". "OK" After that, they left Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think on the afternoon of 26th October you had a meeting in Kiseljak with a local lawyer. In your statement you say something about the atmosphere in Kiseljak at that time. I wondered if you could explain to the court how the atmosphere felt to you in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was there, it was a meeting in the police station, and I met there Mr. Marjanovic. He was the Prosecutor in the Kiseljak, and I met him before because we had to sort something out concerning the status of the force agreement. So I knew that place before, and different from the first time that I went there. I saw a lot of, I do not know if they were soldiers or policemen. It is very difficult to see the difference between policemen and soldiers and sometimes with civilians, because they are very often clothed in kind of devil dress. But it was very tense around the station, and in town I saw rifles, more than usual, and I cannot other than express that I felt the tense much more than before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say Marjanovic was the local Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did he take his instructions from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when we had to -- when we talked before about status of force agreement, I think I have to explain that, what is a status forces agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please do, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The status of forces agreement is a kind of document where the legal position of UN soldiers, where it all is arranged in those papers. It is a basic document how, to be there, in fact, to be in that area. The problem was that status of forces agreement was signed by President Izetbegovic and, of course, we had to do officially only with the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but in fact we had to deal with three parts, the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the BiH government, of course, and the Republic of Srpske. We had to sort something out from that status of forces agreement, and in that meeting that we had, so before 26th October, they told me that they did not recognise that status of forces agreement because of the fact that the President Izetbegovic had signed it; they had nothing to do with President -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Prosecutor and the people who were present down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From whom was the Prosecutor taking his instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Mostar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Mostar which was the capital of the Croatian community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in fact, I had to deal over there with the Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not with Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think on 26th October 1993 in the evening there was another meeting which took place in the UNPROFOR headquarters; indeed, I think were you going on leave and you sent your assistant, Lieutenant Mike Albers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think Brigadier General Angus Ramsay, the Chief of Staff, was at that meeting as well, was he not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you say in your statement that your assistant came back sweating?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think he instructed you that you have to cancel your leave or, in fact, not instructed you because he was your subordinate, but said: "Colonel, I think you had better cancel your leave"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not quite correct, but the end result was the same; I decided not to go on leave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, I think the next day at 9 o'clock in the morning you set off for Stupni Do in an armoured convoy from Kiseljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you picked up armoured personnel carriers in Visoko from the Canadian battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also the press?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you, first of all, went to Dabravine which is a small village nearby Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where you were briefed by local Bosnian government officials on what they thought had happened in Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just explain to the court what they said to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember that a female mayor was there. She told us what had happened, and there was someone from the Bosnian Army, and, well, they both explained what had happened down there. They said: "Well, a massacre had took place in that village of Stupni Do, and we are very much afraid that many people have been killed down there". They knew that the several people, well, that a lot of people might have been able to fled to the forest and perhaps still were there, but they explained to us what in their view had happened. Then Colonel Alstrom and me, myself, we told them who we were, and specially I remember that we told that we would collect all the information to hand it over later on to the commission of experts. I remember that they were very pleased with that information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think a girl or a young woman arrived at the scene; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I do not know exactly the age.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was she doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She was crying. She was terribly upset and I heard, I did not ask, but I heard, that she escaped from that massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you then left Dabravine and proceeded to Stupni Do; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think on the way you state that there were was shelling and you said something about that shelling in your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was very much nearby and we had to stop, and at the same time I had the impression that the Bosnian Croats were trying, well, to stop us and to prevent us from going on. But it stopped and, well, we went, we went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I think you came to Stupni Do or, in fact, outside Stupni Do to a tunnel under a railway; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think there you were stopped at a checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was controlling that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were two HVO soldiers under that tunnel, and they both had a rifle. We were allowed to carry on but without press. The press had to leave. But I think that near the tunnel, the soldiers of NORDBAT took the escort over from CANBAT or the Canadian battalion. I remember that the first car was an armoured carrier from the Danish platoon. The platoon's commander said: "OK, we have to, everybody, all the cars are going to" -----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go in a convoy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To go in a convoy, so ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very close?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- very close together and then he said: "We go, regardless what those soldiers will say, we go" and we went. So the soldiers were a little bit surprised because of that attitude because they were not quite used to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you know that they were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I could see it on their signs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The badge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the red spots.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The badge with the red spots?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The checkerboard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian checkerboard flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, as you say, you proceeded on your way in a close convoy into Stupni Do. What was your immediate impression of the village when you got there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I saw that village I saw that it was, it was a complete massacre, well, all the houses were burned down and torn down and it was not a nice view. At the same time I looked around and I thought, well, it is very easy to do that because it was a kind of, it was a kind of bowl, completely hidden from the outside world. You had the impression that people could do anything in such a place without knowledge of the outside world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without anybody, indeed, seeing what had happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was in Stupni Do when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were soldiers of, Swedish soldiers ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Swedish soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- yes, with armoured carriers and I saw soldiers from BRITBAT.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: BRITBAT being the British battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, BRITBAT, sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you also met the French UNMO to whom you earlier referred, Lieutenant Colonel Patrick Martin, and I understand that he showed you around the village; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the court what he showed you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the first thing that he showed me was a house and we went in. I remember that there was something, a kind of a room with food, and it was rather dark, and there was a kind of sweet smell and I smell the burning things, the smell of fire, and sweet smell, I do not know, it is very difficult to -- I went in and in the end someone had a torch and then I saw three women in a corner in a kind of box. I do not remember if it was a hole in a corner or it was -- but I remember there was a lid to it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not remember whether it as was a box standing on the ground?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, or on the same level, or under it, a cellar or something, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. Did you see anything else in the village at all? I know you have described the destruction but did you see any more remains of human bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that there was a kind of a house without a roof. We were able to look inside because there was a kind of road, and the road was on the same level as the roof. The roof had disappeared. So we were able to look inside and there we saw, I think, four burned bodies. There was another house where I saw, where I saw a burned body as well. They told that it was a child, but it was not to be seen. I saw the man, a man before a house with a kind of wooden tree over him with a beard. He was lying on his back. I see a man who was up the hill. He lay on his, on his breast, an old man. Of course, if you ask me about human beings, that is what ---

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- I remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you spend in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The whole afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then, I think, you returned from Stupni Do to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, I think you then went on leave back to the Netherlands; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you returned from the Netherlands to Kiseljak on 15th November 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, am I correct in saying, that you were made aware that representations had been made from the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council General Staff in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that you had been made aware that certain representations had been made by the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, to the headquarters in Mostar regarding Stupni Do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not quite understand the word "representations".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Representations" means a message or -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Koet says you are talking like a lawyer!

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I apologise, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You know I am a lawyer as well, so .....

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I will rephrase the question. Did the HVO general staff in Mostar make some form of communication with the headquarters in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, regularly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe they made a communication about Stupni Do; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they say about Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came back I heard that the HVO would like to co-operate with -- they were, of course, very much aware of the fact that we did a lot of investigations in that massacre, and they wanted to co-operate with us in that investigation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I think, indeed, you actually had a meeting at 10 o'clock on 22nd November at 1993 at the UN Protection Force headquarters in Kiseljak. With whom was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Liaison Officer, Vinko Lucic, who was regularly as HVO representative in headquarters, was there together with a man in uniform, in a kind of battle dress, whose name was Ivan Bandic. Mr. Bandic appeared to be the legal adviser of the headquarters in Mostar. We had an interpreter named Renata.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let me get this absolutely correct. The two people at that meeting were, firstly, the liaison officer from the HVO who was permanently based at Kiseljak, that is, Vinko Lucic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but not based on the headquarters -- at least not when I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right, so he would come to the headquarters and liaise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ivan Bandic who was a Legal Officer from Mostar, from the HVO General Staff headquarters in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you kept notes of this meeting, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed, I think you produced a memorandum of that meeting; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 21? 21. Do you recognise that document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because of my signature, because I remember I made this document myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Indeed. I think this is a memorandum produced from the notes of your meeting on 22nd November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you read it out to the court, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. "Subject: First report meeting in connection with the Stupni Do incident".

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 21 will be admitted then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "On November 22, 1993, I had a meeting with Colonel Vinko Lucic and an investigator from HVO headquarters in Mostar, Mr. I. Bandic. They wished assistance in investigating the Stupni Do incident. HVO was willing to cooperate with UNPROFOR. After I had introduced myself, Mr. Bandic did. He was a military lawyer. He advised the army staff on military legal matters such as war crimes and abuse of human rights. I told them that extensive investigations had been taking place and still were going on. An interim report had already been forwarded to the War Crimes Commission in Geneva. I asked them then if they already had received an extract of that report (without names, with only general circumstances). As they had not, I promised them a copy of this extract in the English language. Mr. Bandic stated that the attack on the village of Stupni Do ought to be seen in a military setting. He would give a further statement on this subject in a second meeting. He agreed, however, that this could not justify the things that had happened in the village. I asked Mr. Bandic what happened with Mr. Rajic, the commander of the unit that committed the war crimes. I was told that he was revoked, that he was given some 'advisory jobs'. I then said that even Croatian newspapers declared that the army staff of the HVO took the responsibility for the attack on Stupni Do. The name of Ivica Rajic was to be the responsible commander. According to Mr. Bandic, it was not sure if Mr. Rajic was aware of the attack on the village. We agreed to meet again on November 27th 1993."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then I think it is signed "J W Koet", indeed by yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you understand the meaning of the word "revoked" when Mr. Bandic said that to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that he was being sacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is how you understood that to mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you believe that at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you not believe it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we heard already that he was walking around in Kiseljak in his military outfit and that he still was in charge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think a second meeting took place on 27th November 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think, indeed, you kept notes of that meeting as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you put those notes again into the form of a memorandum. If the witness could be shown Prosecutor's Exhibit 22? If you could look at that document? Do you recognise it as a photographic copy of an original document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a document that I wrote myself and it is signed by me as my document, a copy of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecutor's Exhibit 22 be admitted into evidence please, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, Prosecutor's Exhibit 22 will be admitted, a letter dated November 30th 1993 signed by Lieutenant Colonel Koet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could you read the memorandum out to the court, please, Colonel Koet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Subject: Second report meeting in connection with the Stupni Do incident. Reference: First report meeting in connection with the Stupni Do incident No. 241101 jwk dated November 24th 1993. On November 27th 1993 a second meeting took place between Mr. Bandic and Colonel Lucic on the one side and the undersigned on the other side in connection with the Stupni Do incident. First, Mr. Bandic handed over a handwritten letter about alleged war crimes committed by MOS 'attached'. Then Mr. Bandic said that he had statements of soldiers who took part in the attack on Stupni Do. He then explained that Stupni Do was important for the HVO from a military point of view: Stupni Do was controlled by BiH. The village was situated on the road between the Croatian villages Vares and Mir/Planica. Before the beginning of the war 50 Serb inhabitants were expelled by the Muslims. In August 1993 a man called Miocevic, nickname 'Beli', was killed in Stupni Do by A Janovic, from BiH, from the village Myakovici. From then on the situation apparently worsened. The BiH started to fortify the elevation of BOGOS (trenches and so on). From here one has a view of Stupni Do. From this hill they fired weapons into HVO controlled areas so now and then. During the same time the village of Kopjari as well as the elevation of Lijesnica was taken over by BiH. The western part of the Vares community was controlled by MOS and (from Kakanj). The village of Stupni Do is situated south of Vares. Taking this all into account, HVO wanted to take over Stupni Do. The initial plan, however, was to take over the elevation of Bogos. The attack on the elevation of Bogos started on October 22nd 1993, and lasted about four hours. In the meantime the BiH as well as the inhabitants of Stupni Do were able to leave the village. The HVO had information that the BiH from Stupni Do requested their HQ in Budozelje to withdraw, which was refused. From the top of the elevation Bogos it was to be seen that the defence was less strong than had been expected. The attack started in the morning of October 23rd 1993. Mr. Bandic admitted that, apparently, phosphorus ammunition was used. However, he stated, HVO soldiers saw citizens of Stupni Do set fire to their own houses, apparently, to prevent HVO from using these. Women were shooting on HVO soldiers and in some cases BiH soldiers killed themselves to prevent them from being arrested. The HVO soldiers were told not to shoot at civilians. Two of them did not obey the orders. Those names are known. Mr. Bandic stated that they had a video tape with trenches and fortifications of Stupni Do just before the attack. If he became aware of further details, he would inform us. I then asked if it was possible to speak with soldiers of the HVO unit that attacked Stupni Do. That was not possible. After this I asked if he could give me the names of the two soldiers that shot at civilians. He could not give me the names. When I told Mr. Bandic that especially the details concerning the attack on Stupni Do did not seem very plausible, he just said that those were the statements of the soldiers that were involved. In the end, I repeated our concern about role of Mr. Rajic. Mr. Bandic still stated that he was revoked but that he was given advisory jobs. It appeared to me that HVO could not miss his (pure) military skills. We agreed to meet again, if necessary. Gl Legal J W Koet, Lieutenant-Colonel", and signed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Signed by you?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask just two questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is "MOS"? What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, not any more the abbreviation. It is an abbreviation of a kind of extreme Muslim group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: OK. Bogos -- B-O-G-O-S -- was that a part of the village of Stupni Do, just an area within Stupni Do, only higher up or a different ------

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, yes, I think it was something higher -- I do not know, I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I can assist you there, your Honour. It was, in fact, a hill above Stupni Do, Bogos.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But a part of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It was a part of Stupni Do. It was a hill that overlooks the village. Yes. (To the witness): Colonel Koet, referring to paragraphs 13 to 15 of that memorandum, which is where Mr. Bandic states that -- in fact, correction, paragraphs 12 and 13 -- in fact, the citizens of Stupni Do set fire to their own houses; women were shooting on HVO soldiers and, in fact, Bosnian soldiers killed themselves to prevent them from being arrested. I think you got rather angry at this point, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you get angry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if you are trying to find an excuse for a massacre as such, you have to find a very good excuse and this was very much made up. They tried to give a kind of justification for what they did, and this was a really ridiculous one, what they told, what they told us, what they told me, and it was very hard for me just to write that down and to do as if nothing special had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So because it sounded so ridiculous you thought it was made up; is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Vinko Licic saying anything at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he looked very much -- he was very, well, he pretended as if he was not interested at all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask one question. Why did you think it was ridiculous? Why do you think it was made up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we saw the result of that massacre, and there were a lot of people killed. We discovered, I think, 16 dead bodies in that village there. There was not any sign that soldiers killed themselves and it does not make any sense.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not kill themselves, what about burning down their houses so that the HVO would not occupy them; why did you consider that to be ridiculous?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that the first thing you try to do is to flee and not to set fire in your own house -- under those circumstances then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Stupni Do, in your opinion, important from a military point of view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: None at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because it was totally isolated, a totally isolated place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was not on the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no main road, not at all. It was, as I told you, it was in a bowl. It was a farming community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it on the road from Vares to Tuzla, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no main road. It was, if you come out of this region, you can -- you do not expect villages like that. It was in the middle of nowhere. The village was in the middle of nowhere. That is what I thought.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the G2 intelligence person you mentioned earlier tell you anything about the attack upon which you based your conclusion that it was ridiculous, what Mr. Bandic was telling you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not discussed and, as far as I know, they did not try to find out -- they did not even try to find out if it, if that made up story made sense.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think there the meeting ended, did it not, Colonel? I do not think you had any further meetings with representatives of the HVO General Staff in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you then returned to the Netherlands. When did you return to the Netherlands from ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my mission?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- your mission in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think about 1st 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Colonel. No further questions, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We have no further questions. You may be excused, Colonel -- is it Colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, thank you so much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have no further witnesses, your Honour. I was going to propose to the court that I close now, unless you specifically want me to read out in public the measures that were taken by the Prosecutor to serve the indictment and arrest warrant?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: I imagine that you are also relying upon all the other statements in the first batch and in the second batch as supporting your prima facie case, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: May I ask one question? Are the witnesses A to G alive?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A to G are, indeed, alive, yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Did you have any summons served on them for Rule 61 proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, we did not, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Because it was decided at the time that, indeed, the security risks to them for this hearing are far too extreme. Indeed, for the trial it would be our intention to call them, but in order to make these people live through the nightmare of 23rd October 1993, I would only recommended to this office that we do that once and only once. Those are my views.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Please explain to us. There is a matter regarding the question of the Rule 61 which I would like now to discuss with you. How I look at the matter, I will explain. I may be wrong. If I am wrong, you will kindly correct me, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: My reading may be distorted perhaps, you know, somewhat rigid on conventional lines or something like that. As I read the rules regarding prima facie case, when it comes for first confirmation and it comes before the three judges in an open court for further reconfirmation, I would understand it something like this, that the word "witness" there means a witness who is the witness whom you will be producing at the trial for the proof of the case. Mr. Ehsan Bajwa is only an amanuensis. He is not a witness. He has only just recorded a statement. But he has come and he has given his statement as if he was speaking like a witness. How do you account for that? You could have said: "The witnesses A to G are very important. I am sorry, we do not want to produce them here for security reasons. We would like that they should remain alive at least until the day the accused decides to turn up and a formal trial will begin. For the present, we rely upon their statements", and that would be sufficient. But how does Ehsan Bajwa come in as an amanuensis and says: "He told me this, he told me that, she told me that", and he is giving testimony, almost a secondary testimony, of the same witness. That, I think, is not permitted under Rule 61. You are permitted to say: "Yes, here is their statement; it is secret".

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: With respect, your Honour, I disagree. The reason why Mr. Bajwa was called to give his evidence is because he was the investigator who took the statements. I agree with you, from a common law point of view, what he said before this Chamber was hearsay; it was the repetition of something that had been said to him. However, I believe that by him giving evidence, it brings those statements alive before the court because he had an experience of those individuals from whom he took the statements. Indeed, I could have read those statements out before the court, but I was not at the interview. It was my view that it would lend some form of credibility to those statements by calling Mr. Bajwa, the investigator, to testify as to what those witnesses had told him in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Does that not make it an invidious distinction, because in that case the statements of the other witnesses are also there. Why did you not call every investigator to say: "He said the same, he said the same, he said the same"? Then you are now having two sets of statements; one at the higher level because Mr. Bajwa has come and of other witnesses who are more important witnesses, perhaps, but for whom no investigator has come.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are right. I mean, I would have liked to have called the actual witnesses themselves but, as I have said to you before, the safety considerations were such that I simply did not want to place people's lives at risk by calling them for what is, in effect, a pretrial hearing. The other witnesses were perfectly prepared to come here and testify as to what they had said to the investigators. Indeed, I could have called investigators for every single one. But, you are quite right, your Honour, the live witness is a much better person to have here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Is there any Rule which permits such a type of situation like this? Do the Rules permit you to call an amanuensis to strengthen something -- you could straightaway say -----

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the Rules of Evidence for the Tribunal, as we discussed before in the original confirmation hearing, are fairly broad. Indeed, in fact, Rule 89(C) states that, "A Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value". In fact, I noticed with some interest this morning that under Rule 89(D): "A Chamber may exclude evidence if its probative value is substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial", which would seem to indicate that in the Rule 61 proceedings the court has no power to exclude evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: We are not excluding evidence in that sense. I did not say I was wanting to exclude evidence. What I was thinking is this, that statements of witnesses are there recorded by one of your officers. It is assumed that he has the power and ability to record. So all the statements which are on the record are statements which we definitely will read if you have produced them. What is the probative value will depend on what he has stated. The only thing which seems somewhat a little strange was this, that an amanuensis had to come only to just repeat something else, merely because it was your contention that for certain serious reasons of concern regarding their security you did not want to produce them, and you did not produce them. We are not binding to you produce everybody, and that if you did not we would hold something out against you and, therefore, to protect yourself you are saying: "Well, let us call, you know, an investigator to protect ourselves and say: 'Yes, yes, I recorded their statement'." It was this feature which was worrying me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand your concerns, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: It is not that we are saying it has no probative value. The statement is there. We are accepting the whole statement as it is. These are, basically, I would say that your statements of A to G, as they are recorded, have stronger probative value, perhaps, than the somebody to which they are given. But since they have come, we have that type of feeling that it is supportive, that the gentleman has come himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: It certainly gives corroboration, does it not, that the actual investigator is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: But not in amanuensis; he cannot add more to the probative value than the statement itself, nor grant credibility because he has recorded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I will bear that in mind for the future.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me just state what I feel about the applicability of the Rules of Evidence. The Rules of Evidence, 89(A), provides: "The Rules of evidence set forth this Section shall govern the proceedings before the Chambers. The Chambers shall not be bound by national rules of evidence. I personally consider that a Rule 61 proceeding is a proceeding and I think that the Rules of Evidence apply. The Rules of Evidence, Rule 89, is in the Section of the Rules of Evidence regarding proceedings before the Tribunal. Rule 61 is not in that Section. It is in an earlier section, but I consider this to be a Rule 61 is a proceeding before a Trial Chamber, and I think that the Rules of Evidence, at least it can be argued, should apply. The problem though, and they may not apply, well, the problem is not that they may not apply, but the problem is that this is basically a public confirmation of the indictment. When you then present the indictment to a confirming judge, of course, that is not a proceeding. Then, of course, the Rules of Evidence, I presume, would not apply when you, for example, presented the evidence to Judge Sidhwa, the Rules of Evidence. Now, though, we are here at a public proceeding and the question then becomes whether the Rules of Evidence apply. I think a good argument can be made that they would apply, but I do not know whether that would mean that we would exclude the testimony of the investigator because of any our 10 Rules of Evidence. The problem that I have is that Rule 61 says that, "The Prosecutor may also call before the Trial Chamber and examine any witness whose statement has been submitted to the confirming judge". The statement of the investigator had not been submitted to the confirming judge. But then in 61(C), the first sentence says: "If the Trial Chamber is satisfied on that evidence", referring to the previous paragraph, "together with such additional evidence as the Prosecutor may tender, that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the accused has committed all or any of the crimes charged in the indictment, it shall so determine". So that seems to envision that there is the possibility of additional evidence that may be offered. Whether that "additional evidence" phrase modifies that contained in the last sentence of 61(B) is a question, but it is something that we discussed among ourselves, as a Trial Chamber, before we began. I personally think that it does, but I agree with Judge Sidhwa that, from a technical point of view, having an investigator here to summarise what is said really does not lend more credibility. It does, though, make a better presentation of evidence, because if you are going to read at length from these statements, sometimes it is difficult to hold the attention of the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But, in terms of credibility -- not credibility, but in terms of the weight that should be given to the evidence, I agree with Judge Sidhwa; it does not really lend anything. But I think that we need to look at the juxtaposition -- is that the term that intellectuals use -- between 61(B) and 61(C) to see where we are. I think it is his testimony, though, was admissible as additional evidence, even though, clearly, he did not have a statement that had been submitted to the confirming judge. That also applies to the statement of Lieutenant Colonel Koet because was that not a new statement? That had not been submitted ---

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: There is a slight problem there.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- and the photographer, Bernard Petterson.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Bernard Petterson, indeed, there was not a statement submitted with the original bundle. With Lieutenant Colonel Jan Koet, there was a summary statement submitted that was originally taken by the United Nations Protection Force. But, indeed, at the last hearing Justice Sidhwa made an observation that he was only prepared to accept statements that had been taken -- I think, actually this was specifically in respect of eyewitnesses by Tribunal investigators. Indeed, these UN Protection Force statements were summaries and they were not really very satisfactory. So we corrected the position by taking a full statement ourselves from Lieutenant Colonel Jan Koet. So the court was, in fact, on notice of the existence of the witness, Colonel Koet, but indeed had not seen the full statement.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We certainly have the full statements of Petterson and Koet now and coming in as additional evidence under 61(C) -- under 61(C), I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: The evidence of Koet and the photographer is correct, because you are stating: "They are our witnesses" and you are producing them. I was only just referring to the fact of the amanuensis in that sense, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I do understand, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: It does not add to the weight of value or anything, and I would have been content to say: "Here are the statements. We are keeping it secret. We do not want to produce them for security reasons". We would read them. You do not have to read it out if you think that identification would be disclosed, but they are based on the statements. They are statements of ocular witnesses. What more can you get?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which is what you required last time, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: We are not throwing out your evidence. What I am saying is how does this chap figure in as an amanuensis, trying to -- you were perhaps more afraid of yourself, you see, than anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I understand your point, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I think I ought to also to add my voice to what has been said. We had a discussion on this matter and I would like to associate myself with the remarks made by Judge Sidhwa on the technical nature of evidence which you have submitted through the investigator. I think it is something, perhaps, you will have to consider for future proceedings. But, following on that, I would like to find out from you whether the type of evidence which the investigator gave in our proceedings was given also in previous Rule 61 procedures?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I believe it was, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: It was, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think we would like to hear from you, Mr. Cayley, regarding your efforts to effect service on Mr. Rajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Madam President, your Honours, a report on measures taken by the Prosecutor for personal service of the indictment and warrant of arrest was served on the court on 6th March 1996. I think, possibly, the most appropriate thing for me to do is to simply read out in public the measures that were, indeed, taken by the Prosecutor. That begins at paragraph 5, Registry page 296. The measures taken to effect service and the facts pertaining to this issue are the following: On 29th August 1995, an indictment against Ivica Rajic was confirmed by Judge Rustam Sidhwa and warrants for the accused's arrest were issued being directed to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Registrar document Nos. 220 to 224 inclusive and Registrar document No. 230 to 234 inclusive. On 8th December 1995, a warrant for the accused's arrest was issued by Judge Vohrah being directed to the Republic of Croatia, Registrar document Nos. 240 to 244 inclusive. At the time of filing this report, no State to whom an arrest warrant has been transmitted has responded. Following a request by the Prosecutor, the Registrar on 29th January 1996 requested the Minister of Justice of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the diplomatic representatives of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to arrange for the publication of the indictment upon Ivica Rajic in newspapers having wide circulation in these States. On 8th February 1996, the Minister of Justice of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina notified the Registrar that the indictment against Ivica Rajic had been advertised on the radio television of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Independent Radio Studio 99, Independent Television 99, Independent Television Hyatt and in Oslobodenje and in Avaz; these last two being daily newspapers with a wide circulation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. On 31st January 1996, Mr. Zvonimir Hodak, a lawyer of Pavla Hatza, Zagreb, in the Republic of Croatia informed the Registrar that he had been instructed to act for Ivica Rajic, and a power of attorney, purportedly signed by Ivica Rajic in Kiseljak on 19th January 1996, was filed at the same time in which Mr. Rajic appointed the said Zvonimar Hodak to act as his lawyer in case No. IT-95-12-1 before the Tribunal. At the time of filing this report, Ivica Rajic has not been arrested. Indeed, the final paragraph simply states that the Prosecutor submits that the requirements of Rule 61(A) of the Rules had been satisfied. That is dated 6th March 1996 and, indeed, signed by my learned friend Mr. Ostberg and by myself.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, there has been a power of attorney filed in this case, has there not, on behalf of Mr. Rajic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are quite right, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: By Mr. Hodak, is it, H-O-D-A-K?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is right, H-O-D-A-K, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The record should reflect that the Registry sent a letter to Mr. Hodak notifying him of this proceeding, advising him that the proceeding is ex parte, and sending him a copy of the Rules, most particularly Rule 65. The Registry has not heard from Mr. Hodak, have we?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No. He has been present at the Tribunal because he is representing another accused at the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But with respect to this proceeding, has he filed anything?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, with respect to this, I can just confirm that he filed a power of attorney and we sent -- that he has been notified.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, I think, your Honour, he was actually occupying one of the front row seats yesterday at the proceedings, but I do not think he is here today.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have you heard from Mr. Hodak, the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: We have because, in fact, my learned friend Mr. Ostberg did, in fact, send him a copy of the indictment in respect of Rajic. Indeed, he acknowledged that indictment, so that was as well as the Registry sending him notification of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: But beside that we have not heard anything from him in this case.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Pardon me?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: We have not heard anything else from him.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And a warrant for arrest has not been executed?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: The fact that he has been served does not figuratively make the accused present in court for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No, I understand not, your Honour, no, because it is an ex parte proceeding so .....

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley or Mr. Ostberg or both, you may proceed to present your closing, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is fairly irregular, what I am about to do, but if I can ask for your permission? I understand there was probably yesterday some misunderstanding about brigades and structures. Indeed, the evidence is contained in the bundles. I wondered if could I try to explain to you, do you mind if I step over to the board and try to explain to you the structure of the military units?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No, no problem. I welcome all of the assistance I can get.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am not actually giving evidence before the Tribunal because all of the statements which actually support what I am about to tell you are, indeed, contained in the original bundle and the subsequent bundle. The unit that we have been talking about is this, the Bobovac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can that be seen? Can the public see that? I think there is some concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. FEATHERSTONE
utterances.text: Excuse me, I think the concern may also be that you may not be going through the microphone for the interpretation and recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: The HVO, effectively, the military wing of the Croatian community of Herzeg-Bosna, as we understand it and, indeed, as the evidence is in the bundles before you, had a Central Bosnian Operational Zone. The headquarters of the Central Bosnian Operational Zone was in Vitez which is a small town near Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: How do you spell that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: V-I-T-E-Z. The Operational Zone had three groups underneath it, so the three groups were with the constituent military units of the Central Bosnian Operational Zone. We know that Ivica Rajic was the commander of the second operational group whose headquarters was based at Kiseljak where, indeed, Lieutenant Colonel Jan Koet said he was stationed with the United Nations Protection Force headquarters. Interestingly, they were co-located, not in the same building, I hasten to add, but indeed in the same place. The second operational group had three brigades underneath it; one in Sarajevo, one in Kiseljak, and one in Vares. The one in Vares was called the Bobovac Brigade. I cannot remember off the top of my head the number of the statement in the first bundle, but the individual that Colonel Henricsson referred to, Major Hakan Birger, who was Colonel Henricsson's Company Commander in Vares -- so he was in charge of the local UN military unit in Vares -- he met the commander of the Bobovac Brigade on 7th October. He says in his statement that the commander of the Bobovac Brigade was a man called Emil Hara. If you remember, Colonel Henricsson said that this unit, it was understood at the time, formally came under the command of the Bosnian Army, of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But, in reality, it came under the command of the second operational group. It does sound peculiar, but the reason for it, from what Major Birger says, is because this was an isolated area, and the Bosnian Croats, for whatever reason, felt that they needed to be in an alliance with the Bosnian government. But, in reality, Colonel Henricsson said to you yesterday that, in fact, the Bobovac Brigade came under the command of Ivica Rajic in Kiseljak. Indeed, you heard the evidence that Ivica Rajic came to Vares on or about 23rd October and, in effect, took direct command of a subordinate unit that was in the area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Rajic took over then the Bobovac Brigade command; when would that have been?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: On the evidence, your Honour, and obviously without me giving evidence, but based on the statements before you, that would be on or before 23rd October.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: And the commander before, was he a Bosnian Croat?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He was.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But at some point before, I gather, before he was the commander of the Bobovac Brigade, you are saying that that brigade was controlled by the Bosnians?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He was always the brigade commander but, in effect -- if I could sort of draw a line in -- the command went to the 2nd Bosnian corps. I think it is the 2nd -- it is in Henricsson's testimony -- that was based in Tuzla. So the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had a corps headquarters that was based in Tuzla, and Emil Hara acknowledged then, it seems, from what he told the witnesses that we have interviewed, that the Bobovac Brigade was under this command although, in reality, as Henricsson said, it came under the command of Ivica Rajic in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is when the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnians were allies?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That, I cannot answer because there is nothing in the statements to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: But, at least, Colonel Henricsson does say that the commander before Rajic ---

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Emil Hara.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- reported -- Hara -- to the 2nd Bosnian ------

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is what he believes. That is what he was told.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is what he believes. I am sure he believes all of what he said, OK, that is for sure. OK, but certainly after the time that Rajic took over, there was not that reporting to the Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Absolutely, your Honour. Does the Bench have any questions?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Has that made things clearer?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. It makes something clearer in that in Ekenheim's statement -- I think it was in Ekenheim's statement -- he said that he felt that the attack on Stupni Do -- correct me if I am wrong -- was to create dissention, to use a mild word, between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnians.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Indeed, that is what was suggested.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That he believed that, in fact, they were close, too close, and if the predecessor to Rajic was reporting to the Bosnian corps, 2nd Bosnian corps, that would seem to fit in with his testimony; that there was a relationship at that time between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnians. But when Commander Rajic took over that was not the case, and at least it is Mr. Ekenheim's belief that that is why Stupni Do was attacked, but in any case go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In closing, I, first of all, intend, your Honours, to give a brief summary of the evidence you have heard, and then, indeed, address the questions of International Humanitarian Law and -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Can I ask one question before your begin your arguments? What is the effect of this group of people being in Kiseljak? You call them occupational force or something?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Which force?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Croat occupational force? What is the position of this Kiseljak territory ---

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: -- or Vares which is, basically, in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Now some group is there after the Croats, you call it a pocket group, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In reality, the position was -----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: Will you treat this group as not in occupational force of Croats or as an occupational force of Croats? I want the technical position from you, because the question then would arise, who is the protected person and things -----

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: You are absolutely right, your Honour. I am going to cover this in my closing. Could I please do it in order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SIDHWA
utterances.text: So long as you are on notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I am aware, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I have just one question as it relates to your outline? The Bobovac Brigade, you have under that Vares, but that includes the area of Stupni Do?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour. I think, as Lieutenant Colonel Koet indicated to you -- I mean, I have indeed been, I know I should not be giving evidence before this court, but it is, in fact, off a track off the main road, that is the reality, although it was in the municipality of Vares, because Vares itself was not only the town of Vares, but the municipal area. In fact, Vares was the municipal town. It was like the state, sort of, the municipal capital for that area.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You are not really give evidence. You are giving now, as far as I am concerned, your closing summary. At least in my system, we always tell the jurors, at least, that what the lawyers say is not evidence; they are just giving their version of what the evidence showed. So, as far as I am concerned, I am listening to what you consider to be your version of what the evidence showed and it is helpful to me, but I will look at the statements, that is for sure, and recall the transcript. But I just wanted to add (and also not giving evidence), that you say Bobovac Brigade, Vares, but that is the area from the testimony, as I recall, that would cover Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Firstly, I will give the court a very brief, what I hope is a brief, summary of the evidence. Firstly, you heard from Mr. Ehsan Bajwa. I will not be too long, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It was so interesting; we were just going to go ahead and we forgot that, perhaps, a recess might be in order particularly for the reporter there who is busily at work, so we will stand in recess for 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Madam President, your Honours, first of all, I will give you a brief summary of the evidence that you have heard and then move on to deal with other matters. Firstly, you heard from Mr. Eshan Bajwa, a Tribunal Investigator. He recounted to you the statements of six eyewitness survivors from the attack on Stupni Do. I know that concerns have already been expressed by you about introducing this form of evidence. I had dealt with it in my closing, but I believe we have now discussed all the matters you have raised already, so I will not continue with that. So what did Mr. Bajwa tell you? Firstly, he recounted to you the statement of Witness A contained in the additional bundle of evidence served as an exhibit by the Registry on the court. Witness A, as you remember, was the President of the local community in Stupni Do. He was shown an aerial photograph of Stupni Do and identified the photograph as being of Stupni Do, and in fact identified virtually every structure on the photograph together with the owner of that structure. That photograph is Prosecutor's Exhibit 1. I know yesterday there was some confusion between the words "village" and "hamlet". "Hamlet" unfortunately is a very English word. The distinction is simply this. A village is larger than a hamlet. When indeed I was referring to "hamlet" I was referring to a part of the village. In fact in Witness A's statement he first of all describes a part of the village as being a "hamlet" and then he describes it as "part of", but that indeed is the distinction that was intended between "village" and "hamlet". Indeed Witness A identifies 13 different hamlets within this village. I know, Justice McDonald, you were particularly interested in the number of dwellings in the village. Witness A identified 66 separate dwellings and numerous stables and utility buildings belonging to the residents. I do not believe that Mr. Pettersen was mistaken when he provided to you a lower figure yesterday. I think that simply when he arrived there was utter devastation in the village and it was very difficult for him to assess properly the number of buildings in the village. Second, there was a part of the village called Lipa which was in the direction of another Croat village called Mir, and that could not actually be seen where from Mr. Pettersen took that photograph. It certainly would not have been immediately visible to him in the locality of the village where he was situated. Witnesses B to F all confirm the time and date of the attack: 8 o'clock in the morning on 23rd October 1993. Witnesses B, C and D provide compelling evidence of events in the hamlet of Pricado. You will remember Mr. Pettersen referring to this area of the village as an "upper part" of the village of Stupni Do; it was raised above the rest of the village. These three witnesses state that a group of civilians were forced from the basement shelter of Witness A's house by soldiers. Witnesses C and D both identified the soldiers as displaying the Croatian checkerboard flag, and Witness C clearly remembers seeing the letters "HVO" on the soldiers' shoulder badges, at least on one of the soldiers' shoulder badges. Witness B states seeing a white ribbon around the upper arm of the soldiers entering the basement. You will recall that Sergeant Ekenheim stated yesterday that he had been told by a survivor that soldiers from outside the area carried out the attack on Stupni Do. Sergeant Ekenheim further stated that the unit was dressed either in camouflage or black and wore ribbons so that they could recognise each other in combat. Witnesses C and D speak of soldiers in camouflage-style uniforms. Witness F recalls seeing soldiers in black uniforms with a white ribbon tied around their upper arm. All these witnesses recount in detail the murder of three men and one woman. All victims are similarly identified by name. All three witnesses recalled being locked into a summer kitchen or shed which was set on fire. All recall the break-out by Witness B using an axe to open the door. Witness C recalls in his statement that he remembers soldiers throwing the four dead bodies into a burning house. You will remember that it was in this very area where Mr. Pettersen photographed four severely burnt bodies; one being identified as that of a woman and one being identified as that of a man by the Swedish doctor who subsequently arrived in the village. You recall that both witnesses B, C and D state that they escaped to Pajtov Han, a small village near to Stupni Do. Once there they said that they were captured by local HVO. When UNPROFOR, the UN Protection Forces, tried to assist them, the UNPROFOR were told that they needed to seek permission from Ivica Rajic. They variously referred to as both Rajic and Ivica Rajic. Witness E you will remember is the teenage girl who is shot in the side and then hides in a vegetable pit in the basement of a house with her aunt, sister and woman neighbour. Witness E is hidden beneath the three other women. She hears male voices and then gunfire and then silence. She survives. The other three women are murdered. This witness then escapes from the basement saying first to Mr. Bajwa that in the basement when she went to leave there was a candle burning on the floor near to the pit, "I picked it and blew it out." You will recall Mr. Pettersen's second, third and fourth photographs. One of those photographs shows three dead women in a pit and a red candle to the side of the pit. He recalled how odd he thought it was at the time that there should be a candle present. Brigadier General Henricsson confirms seeing three dead women in a cellar in Stupni Do on 26th October 1993. Sergeant Ekenheim and Lieutenant Colonel Koet confirm the same. During her escape the young woman is shot at in a presumed intent of killing her to prevent her escaping. She does indeed escape into surrounding woods and climbs a tree where she observes almost the entire village in flames. The last witness you heard about was Witness F who was the 44 year old woman who lost both her husband and her son during the attack. She witnesses the death of an elderly gentleman and then tells the investigator the dreadful circumstances about the discovery of her son's death. After capture by the HVO she is forced to go to the remaining members of the village Guard Force to tell them to surrender. She then makes good her escape. I will come back in fact to the matter of the village Guard Force and the relevant statements. Next you heard from Brigadier General Henricsson. He told you that there was heavy fighting between Muslims and Croats in central Bosnia. I suspect here when he said "Croats" he actually meant "Bosnian Croats". He particularly mentioned Gornji Vakuf and Mostar. Fighting broke out between Muslims and Croats, he said, in the Vares area in August 1993. In fact I think he gave a specific date 18th August. You will recall that Brigadier Henricsson was in Vares on 23rd October 1993 and was informed on the way there in the village of Dabravine by Bosnian government authorities of an attack on the village of Stupni Do. You will recall Brigadier General Henricsson met Ivica Rajic in Vares on a number of occasions; in fact on four occasions. Rajic stated to him very clearly that he was the commander of the operational group in Vares and that he was the new commander of the Bobovac Brigade; that he was the commander of the whole area, that is what Brigadier General Henricsson said that Rajic said to him. Brigadier General Henricsson recounted how Rajic refused to let him into Stupni Do; first agreeing to allow entry and then refusing. You recall that Brigadier General Henricsson explained that he had stood on a hill and viewed Stupni Do through binoculars. He observed a burning village and also the sound of small arms fire. Brigadier General Henricsson confirms his entry into the village on 26th October 1993 where he observed a totally destroyed village of 54 houses, where there were dead and burnt bodies. He confirms the rescue of persons who had escaped from Stupni Do. He stated at the end of his evidence that he was absolutely certain, those were his words, that Rajic was in charge of the HVO forces in and after the attack on Stupni Do.
